title: Pretrained Language Models as Visual Planners for Human Assistance
tldr: Names the task: given a goal in words and video of how far the person got, output the remaining steps. Planning for a human, not for a gripper.

problem.task: Visual Planning for Assistance (VPA): goal + progress video → the next actions the person should take.

inputs.name: goal
inputs.chars: One short phrase — "make a shelf".

inputs.name: progress video
inputs.chars: Untrimmed, arbitrarily long, showing what has been done so far.

outputs.name: action plan
outputs.chars: An ordered sequence, evaluated by success rate and mean IoU against the ground-truth remainder.

training.supervision: Segment labels for the observed part, action sequences for the plan.
training.note: Decomposing into segmentation then forecasting is what lets a pretrained LM be dropped into the second half.

method.intuition: Forecasting the rest of a procedure is sequence modeling over actions, which is exactly what a pretrained language model is already good at.
components: multimodal sequence forecasting with an LM
ablations isolating language pretraining, visual input and goal

experiments.headline: Outperforms baselines across plan-quality metrics. Ablations show language pretraining, visual observation and the goal each carry independent weight.

why: The task definition the human-assistance branch has been iterating on ever since.

title: ExpertAF: Expert Actionable Feedback from Video
tldr: A skill score tells you that you are bad. This outputs what to change, in words and as a corrected demonstration of your own body.

problem.task: Generate actionable coaching feedback from a video of someone performing a physical skill.

inputs.name: performance video
inputs.chars: Basketball, soccer, and other skilled activity.

inputs.name: 3D body pose
inputs.chars: Accompanies the video; the correction is expressed in this space.

outputs.name: expert commentary
outputs.chars: Free-form: what is going well, what to change.

outputs.name: expert demonstration
outputs.chars: A generated pose sequence with the correction applied, plus retrieved expert video.

training.supervision: Weakly-supervised pairs built from Ego-Exo4D expert commentary with an LLM.
training.note: Building the training set out of coach commentary is what makes the task learnable at all — nobody annotates corrections directly.

method.intuition: Feedback is only useful if it is executable, so the output has to be a change to the body, not a number.
components: weakly-supervised feedback dataset from expert commentary

experiments.headline: Outperforms strong VLMs on established metrics and in human preference studies across commentary, retrieval and pose generation.

why: The most complete instance of the act stage in a human-embodied loop: the system's output is a change to the person's motion.

title: Vid2Coach: Transforming How-To Videos into Task Assistants
tldr: Watch what rehabilitation therapists actually do when guiding blind cooks, then build the system to do that. Errors drop 58.5%.

problem.task: Turn a how-to video into a wearable-camera assistant that gives accessible instructions and monitors progress.

inputs.name: how-to video
inputs.chars: Offline: the source recipe or tutorial.

inputs.name: live camera
inputs.chars: From commercial smart glasses, streaming.

inputs.name: user speech
inputs.chars: Questions asked mid-task.

outputs.name: instruction
outputs.chars: Augmented with demonstration detail and explicit completion criteria.

training.supervision: No model training — retrieval-augmented generation over BLV-specific resources plus VLM inference.
training.note: The design comes from observing visual rehabilitation therapists, which is the part that generalizes beyond this system.

method.intuition: Video instructions assume visual comparison, so making them accessible means supplying the completion criteria the video leaves implicit.

datasets.name: formative study with visual rehabilitation therapists

experiments.headline: 58.5% fewer errors than participants' typical workflow, with participants wanting to keep using it.

why: The strongest evidence on this list that task guidance is an interaction design problem as much as a perception problem.

title: Satori: Towards Proactive AR Assistant with Belief-Desire-Intention User Modeling
tldr: Most AR assistants wait to be asked. Wiring a BDI user model to a multimodal LLM makes one that decides on its own when to speak, and it matches a hand-tuned Wizard of Oz.

problem.task: Decide when and what to show a user in AR without being asked.

inputs.name: egocentric stream
inputs.chars: From an AR headset during assembly or cooking.

inputs.name: user state
inputs.chars: Beliefs, desires, intentions — inferred, not configured.

outputs.name: AR guidance
outputs.chars: Contextually timed, no heuristics or manual authoring.

training.supervision: None — prompting a multimodal LLM inside a BDI loop.
training.note: The system was designed from two formative studies with twelve experts, so the intervention policy is grounded in practice.

method.intuition: Proactivity requires a model of what the user believes and wants, which is exactly what the BDI framework was built to express — an LLM just makes it inferable from video.

experiments.headline: Matches the Wizard-of-Oz system without manual configuration or heuristics.

why: Puts a name on the hardest open question in human-embodied physical AI: not what to say, but when.

title: eXplainMR: Generating Real-time Textual and Visual eXplanations to Facilitate UltraSonography Learning in MR
tldr: Ultrasound training needs a patient, a probe and an expert. This replaces all three with a headset, a controller and a desk, then explains why the current view is wrong.

problem.task: Real-time formative feedback during cardiac surface ultrasound practice in mixed reality.

inputs.name: probe pose
inputs.chars: Controller standing in for the transducer, desk standing in for the body.

inputs.name: simulated ultrasound image
inputs.chars: Rendered from the slicing plane through an anatomical model.

outputs.name: textual explanation
outputs.chars: Compares the current wrong view to the target view, so the trainee learns why it is wrong.

outputs.name: 3D visual cue
outputs.chars: Shows the intersection of the slicing plane with the anatomy.

training.supervision: None — rule- and model-based feedback over a simulated anatomy.
training.note: Subgoal decomposition into single-movement steps is what makes each explanation actionable.

method.intuition: A trainee who is told the view is wrong learns nothing. Being shown the geometric relationship between the probe and the anatomy is what transfers.

experiments.headline: Supports low-cost anywhere training with automated feedback through four explanation mechanisms.

why: The clinical end of the everyday-to-professional axis, where a wrong action has a cost and explanation becomes mandatory.

title: AROMA: Mixed-Initiative AI Assistance for Non-Visual Cooking by Grounding Multi-modal Information Between Reality and Videos
tldr: Aligns three streams — what the user feels, what the camera sees, and what the recipe video says — so a blind cook can locate themselves inside the procedure.

problem.task: Context-aware assistance for cooking without sight, grounded jointly in the live scene and a reference video.

inputs.name: wearable camera
inputs.chars: Streaming, monitored continuously rather than on request.

inputs.name: video recipe
inputs.chars: The reference the physical state is aligned to.

inputs.name: non-visual cues reported by the user
inputs.chars: Touch, smell, sound — information the camera does not have.

outputs.name: response or alert
outputs.chars: Answers requests and volunteers timely warnings.

training.supervision: None — VLM inference plus alignment logic.
training.note: The user is treated as a sensor as well as a recipient. That is the design move worth stealing.

method.intuition: Neither the person nor the camera has the full state, so the system's job is to reconcile two partial views of the same kitchen.

experiments.headline: A study with eight BLV participants and design implications for interactive AI that supports activities of daily living.

why: The clearest case where the human supplies perception the AI lacks — collaboration inside a single embodiment.

title: ShowHowTo: Generating Scene-Conditioned Step-by-Step Visual Instructions
tldr: Generate the step images conditioned on a photo of the user's own scene, so the instructions are rendered in their kitchen rather than a stock one.

inputs.name: scene image
inputs.chars: The user's actual environment — this is the conditioning that makes it grounded.

inputs.name: textual steps
inputs.chars: The written procedure.

outputs.name: step images
outputs.chars: One per step, consistent with each other and with the input scene.

training.supervision: 0.6M image-text step sequences, mined automatically from 1M instructional videos.
training.note: The mining pipeline is the reusable half — it converts how-to video into supervised step sequences without annotators.

method.intuition: The barrier was never the generator but the absence of paired step-sequence data grounded in a scene, and that pairing can be harvested from video.

experiments.headline: State of the art on all three accuracy dimensions, with code, data and weights released.

why: Visual guidance as generation rather than retrieval — the channel that AR assistance is converging on.

title: VisualChef: Generating Visual Aids in Cooking via Mask Inpainting
tldr: Show what the action looks like and what the object looks like afterwards, by inpainting only the action-relevant objects and leaving the kitchen alone.

problem.task: Given a frame and an action, generate what the action looks like and what the object looks like once it is done.

inputs.name: initial frame
inputs.chars: Egocentric; environment must be preserved.

outputs.name: final state image
outputs.chars: The object after — the part a text instruction cannot convey.

training.supervision: Automatically extracted initial / action / final state frame triplets from egocentric video.
training.note: Mask-based grounding replaces the fine-grained textual descriptions earlier work needed, which removes an annotation dependency.

method.intuition: Regenerating the whole frame throws away the environment the user is standing in. Identify the action-relevant objects and change only those.

experiments.headline: Improves over state-of-the-art methods on three egocentric datasets, quantitatively and qualitatively.

why: Isolates the object-state-change signal inside visual guidance, which is the part that actually tells you whether you did it right.

title: LEGO Co-builder: Exploring Fine-Grained Vision-Language Modeling for Multimodal LEGO Assembly Assistants
tldr: Detecting the brick is solved. Knowing whether the assembly is in the right state is not, and GPT-4o gets 40.5% F1 on it.

problem.task: Stepwise instruction following, object detection and assembly state detection for an AR assembly assistant.

inputs.name: scene
inputs.chars: Programmatically generated multimodal scenes with real LEGO assembly logic.

outputs.name: assembly state
outputs.chars: Whether the build matches the expected state at this step.

training.supervision: Zero-shot and fine-tuned evaluation of existing VLMs.
training.note: Programmatic scene generation gives controlled difficulty, at the cost of some realism.

method.intuition: An assembly assistant fails at state verification, not at object recognition, and a benchmark should separate the two so the failure is visible.

baselines: GPT-4o, Gemini, Qwen-VL, InstructBLIP, MiniGPT-v2, GLM-4.1-thinking
experiments.headline: 98.16% object detection with fine-tuned InstructBLIP, but only 37.52% entity F1 (MiniGPT-v2) and 40.54% state detection F1 (GPT-4o).

why: A precise measurement of the gap between recognizing things and knowing the state of the world, which is what guidance depends on.

title: VideoLLM-online: Online Video Large Language Model for Streaming Video
tldr: A video LLM that decides at each frame whether to speak, rather than being handed a clip and a question after the fact.

problem.task: Temporally aligned dialogue inside a continuous video stream.

inputs.name: video stream
inputs.chars: No lookahead; the model must commit at each frame.

outputs.name: speak-or-wait decision
outputs.chars: The part that distinguishes streaming from offline VideoQA.

training.supervision: Offline temporal annotations converted into streaming dialogue format by a data generation scheme.
training.note: The LIVE objective does language modeling over a continuous stream rather than over a clip.

method.intuition: Treating video as a predetermined clip is what makes video LLMs useless for assistance. The timing of the utterance has to be part of the model's output.

experiments.headline: Over 10 FPS streaming dialogue on a 5-minute clip on one A100, with state-of-the-art results on offline benchmarks too.

why: The enabling piece for every proactive assistant on this list: without streaming, timing cannot be a decision.

title: Grounding Task Assistance with Multimodal Cues from a Single Demonstration
tldr: RGB does not record why someone did something. Gaze and speech from one demonstration recover the intent, and gaze alone gets 93% of what speech gives.

problem.task: Answer a learner's questions about a task using a single recorded demonstration as the reference.

inputs.name: demonstration video
inputs.chars: One pass, egocentric.

inputs.name: gaze
inputs.chars: Implicit intent — where attention went, including to hazards.

inputs.name: speech
inputs.chars: Explicit intent — what the demonstrator said aloud.

outputs.name: answer
outputs.chars: Grounded in retrieved keyframes and captions.

training.supervision: None — retrieval and prompting over the extracted sub-task structure.
training.note: Questions come from real chat-assisted task replication sessions rather than being written for the benchmark.

method.intuition: A frame tells you what happened. Gaze and speech tell you why, and that is what a learner is actually asking about.

baselines: frame-based retrieval without gaze or speech
experiments.headline: Gaze alone reaches 93% of speech-level performance, and the two combined are best. Which cue helps depends on the task type.

why: Argues that human-assistance systems lose their information at the sensing axis rather than at the model.
